name: Behentrimonium chloride
summary: Waxy cationic surfactant that makes conditioners slippery and anti-static; a formulation ingredient rather than a looksmaxxing treatment.
lead: Behentrimonium chloride (also docosyltrimethylammonium chloride, BTAC-228) is a quaternary ammonium compound that acts as a cationic surfactant. It is a yellow, waxlike solid with the formula C25H54ClN.

name: Polyquaternium-10
summary: Cationic cellulose polymer that coats hair in shampoos and conditioners; a background ingredient with no direct trials.
lead: Polyquaternium-10 (PQ-10) is the INCI name for quaternized hydroxyethyl cellulose, a cellulose-derived polymer carrying positively charged quaternary ammonium groups. It belongs to the polyquaternium family, of which at least 40 members have been approved.

name: Cetrimonium chloride
summary: Common conditioner surfactant that detangles and softens hair; a formulation ingredient with documented contact-allergy reports.
lead: Cetrimonium chloride (cetyltrimethylammonium chloride, CTAC) is a quaternary ammonium cationic surfactant, formula C19H42ClN, used in hair conditioners and shampoos and also as an antiseptic. In conditioners it is typically combined with long-chain fatty alcohols such as stearyl alcohol; the mixture forms a lamellar gel with water. Cationic surfactant levels are typically about 1 to 2 percent.

name: Keratin straightening
summary: Salon keratin-and-heat smoothing that lasts months; some products release formaldehyde, and trial data are scant.
lead: Keratin straightening, also called a Brazilian treatment, is a salon smoothing procedure in which a keratin-containing product is applied to the hair and sealed in with a flat iron. Wikipedia describes it as reducing frizz and adding shine, lasting roughly two to six months, and taking about two to four hours.

name: Japanese thermal reconditioning
summary: Salon chemical-plus-heat process that permanently straightens treated hair; no trials found, heat and scalp damage are reported risks.
lead: Japanese thermal reconditioning, also called yuko or rebonding, is a salon procedure for permanently straightening hair. Wikipedia describes a non-coating chemical applied for about 15 to 20 minutes to loosen cysteine bonds, after which heat restructures the hair into a straight form; the full process takes about four to eight hours.

name: Sodium hydroxide relaxer
summary: The classic lye cream that permanently straightens tight curls; strong on straightening, with documented scalp-burn risk and broader health associations under study.
lead: A sodium hydroxide relaxer, commonly called a lye relaxer, is a cream-based chemical hair straightener that uses sodium hydroxide as its active alkali to permanently loosen tight curls. Lye creams typically combine sodium hydroxide, usually at about 5 to 10 percent, with petroleum jelly, mineral oil and emulsifiers, and have a pH of roughly 10 to 14. Relaxers act by breaking disulfide bonds in the hair shaft; the change applies only to treated hair and new growth emerges in its natural texture.

name: Calcium hydroxide relaxer
summary: The 'no-lye' relaxer, billed as gentler on sensitive scalps than lye; no study has shown a different health profile.
lead: A calcium hydroxide relaxer, marketed as a 'no-lye' relaxer, is a chemical hair straightener in which calcium hydroxide (slaked lime) is mixed at the time of use with an activating solution of guanidine carbonate, producing guanidine hydroxide as the active agent. Guanidine hydroxide is described as a weaker alkaline agent than sodium hydroxide, and these products are positioned as an option for sensitive scalps.

name: Macassar oil
summary: The Victorian hair oil that gave us the antimacassar; historically marketed for growth and styling, with no clinical evidence behind the growth claims.
lead: Macassar oil was a scented compound hair oil used mainly by men in Western Europe in the 19th and early 20th centuries to condition and style hair. It was popularised by the London barber Alexander Rowland, who from about 1793 sold Rowland's Macassar Oil, one of the first nationally advertised products. Advertisements made broad claims, including promoting hair regrowth.

name: Jaw surgery / orthognathic
summary: Corrective jaw surgery that repositions the upper jaw, lower jaw and chin for bite, airway and facial-balance goals; a legitimate surgical field that forums treat as the big structural lever.
lead: Orthognathic surgery, also called corrective jaw surgery, reshapes the jaws and lower face to treat structural, growth, airway, jaw-joint and bite problems, and can also be used for facial balance and symmetry. The operation is usually done through the mouth: bone is cut, moved and fixed in a new position, and it is typically coordinated with orthodontic treatment.
claims: Bimax or a single-jaw operation can fix a recessed jaw, and the result is often better than a jaw-jut test suggests.
Jaw surgery carries serious risks that are underreported, including permanent numbness.
Jaw surgery can improve function but disappoint cosmetically.
Getting insurance to cover jaw surgery depends on proving a functional problem.

name: Low-glycemic diet (for acne)
summary: Eating low-GI carbs to calm acne: the one diet tweak with some trial support, though the evidence is modest.
lead: A low-glycemic diet (low-GI or low-glycemic-load diet) is an eating pattern built around foods that raise blood glucose slowly, used by some people with acne in the hope of reducing breakouts. The glycemic index, introduced by David Jenkins and colleagues in 1981, ranks carbohydrate foods from 0 to 100 against pure glucose, and glycemic load adjusts that ranking for portion size.
